claim: Mathys et al. conducted the first single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) study of Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Mathys et al. conducted the first single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq) study of Alzheimer's disease (AD) (Mathys et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mathys et al., 2019

claim: With bulk RNA-seq, changes in gene expression across cell types can be lost, potentially masking the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across different cell types.
source: With bulk RNA-seq, changes in gene expression across cell types can be lost, potentially masking the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across different cell types.
evidence: Based on established understanding of bulk RNA-seq limitations

claim: The reanalysis resulted in 549 times fewer DEGs at a false discovery rate of 0.05 compared to the original study.
source: Here, we correct these issues and use best-practice approaches to snRNA-seq differential expression, resulting in 549 times fewer DEGs at a false discovery rate of 0.05.
evidence: Supported by the authors' reanalysis data presented in the manuscript

claim: Mathys et al. profiled the transcriptomes of approximately 80,000 cells from the prefrontal cortex, collected from 48 individuals – 24 of which presented with varying degrees of AD pathology.
source: The authors profiled the transcriptomes of approximately 80,000 cells from the prefrontal cortex, collected from 48 individuals – 24 of which presented with varying degrees of AD pathology.
evidence: Factual description of the original study design from Mathys et al., 2019

claim: High percentages of mitochondrial reads and low number of reads per cell are indicative of low cell quality.
source: This is indicative of low cell quality (Ilicic et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ilicic et al., 2016

claim: Dataset integration has become a common step in sc-RNA-seq protocols and is recommended to remove confounding sources of variation.
source: As the field has matured since the authors' work was published, dataset integration has become a common step in sc-RNA-seq protocols and is recommended by some to remove confounding sources of variation (Heumos et al., 2023; Amezquita et al., 2020; Tran et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent best-practice guidelines

claim: Reprocessing resulted in 50,831 cells passing QC, approximately 20,000 less than the authors' postprocessing set.
source: Reprocessing resulted in 50,831 cells passing QC, approximately 20,000 less than the authors' postprocessing set with differing cell-type proportions (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data and referenced figures

claim: Over 99% of nuclei had less than 200 genes expressed.
source: With regards to data quality, it is worth noting that over 99% of nuclei had less than 200 genes expressed (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 1

claim: Brase et al.'s recent study of snRNA-seq of autosomal-dominant AD used a more stringent cut-off for the minimum number of expressed genes and still kept 27% (122 times more) of the assayed cells after all QC steps.
source: For example, Brase et al.'s recent study of snRNA-seq of autosomal-dominant AD (Brase et al., 2023) used a more stringent cut-off for the minimum number of expressed genes and still kept 27% (122 times more) of the assayed cells after all QC steps.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brase et al., 2023

claim: The reanalysis used a 10% cut-off for the proportion of mitochondrial reads in a nuclei, as set out in Amezquita et al.'s best-practice guidelines.
source: Our approach used a 10% cut-off for the proportion of mitochondrial reads in a nuclei, as set out in Amezquita et al.'s best-practice guidelines (Amezquita et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to best-practice guidelines

claim: Seurat's guidelines recommend a 5% cut-off for mitochondrial reads.
source: which is less stringent than Seurat's guidelines (5%) (Hao et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hao et al., 2021

claim: Heumos et al., 2023 recommend an 8% cut-off for mitochondrial reads from a median absolute deviations (MAD)-based cut-off selection.
source: or that from Heumos et al., 2023 (8% from a median absolute deviations [MAD]-based cut-off selection)
evidence: Supported by citation to Heumos et al., 2023

claim: Mathys et al. filtered out high mitochondrial read nuclei based on clusters from their t-SNE projection of the data.
source: Conversely, the authors filtered out high mitochondrial read nuclei based on clusters from their t-SNE projection of the data (Mathys et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original Mathys et al., 2019 methods

claim: Over 16,000 nuclei that were removed in the reanalysis QC pipeline were kept by Mathys et al.
source: Even at our lenient cut-off, over 16,000 nuclei that were removed in our QC pipeline were kept by the authors' Figure 2, explaining the discrepancy in the number of nuclei after QC.
evidence: Supported by comparison data shown in Figure 2

claim: High proportions of mitochondrial reads are indicative of cell death.
source: it is clear that the authors' approach was ineffective at removing nuclei with high proportions of mitochondrial reads which is indicative of cell death (Heumos et al., 2023; Ilicic et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Heumos et al., 2023 and Ilicic et al., 2016

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory nuclei with higher than 75% reads from the mitochondria were kept in the final processed dataset by Mathys et al.
source: both excitatory and inhibitory nuclei with higher than 75% reads from the mitochondria were kept in the final processed dataset by the authors.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of the original processed data

claim: Mathys et al. conducted a DE analysis between the controls and the patients with AD pathology, concentrating on six neuronal and glial cell types: excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
source: The authors conducted a DE analysis between the controls and the patients with AD pathology, concentrating on six neuronal and glial cell types; excitatory neurons, inhibitory neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and oligodendrocyte precursor cells, derived from the Allen Brain Atlas (Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to the original study methods and Tasic et al., 2018

claim: Mathys et al. performed a two-part, cell- and patient-level analysis for differential expression.
source: However, for this approach, the authors conducted a two-part, cell- and patient-level analysis.
evidence: Description of the original study's methods

claim: The cell-level analysis took each cell as an independent replicate.
source: The cell-level analysis took each cell as an independent replicate
evidence: Description of the original study's methods

claim: Mathys et al. identified 1031 DEGs using their combinatorial approach requiring an FDR < 0.01 in the cell-level and an FDR < 0.05 in the patient-level analysis.
source: The authors identified 1031 DEGs using this combinatorial approach – DEGs requiring a false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.01 in the cell-level and an FDR < 0.05 in the patient-level analysis.
evidence: Factual description of results from the original study

claim: Cell-level DE approach, also known as pseudoreplication, overestimates the confidence in DEGs due to the statistical dependence between cells from the same patient not being considered.
source: It is important to note that this cell-level DE approach, also known as pseudoreplication, overestimates the confidence in DEGs due to the statistical dependence between cells from the same patient not being considered (Murphy and Skene, 2022; Squair et al., 2021; Zimmerman et al., 2021; Lazic, 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to methodological studies

claim: When inspecting all DEGs identified at an FDR of 0.05 from Mathys et al.'s cell-level analysis, the number increases to 14,274.
source: When we inspect all DEGs identified at an FDR of 0.05 from the authors' cell-level analysis, this number increases to 14,274.
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of the original data

claim: Pseudobulk DE analysis has recently been proven to give optimal performance compared to both mixed models and pseudoreplication approaches.
source: Pseudobulk DE analysis has recently been proven to give optimal performance compared to both mixed models and pseudoreplication approaches (Murphy and Skene, 2022; Squair et al., 2021; Crowell et al., 2020; Soneson and Robinson, 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to methodological comparison studies

claim: Pseudobulk DE analysis aggregates counts to individuals, thus accounting for the dependence between an individual's cells.
source: It aggregates counts to individuals, thus accounting for the dependence between an individual's cells.
evidence: Description of the pseudobulk method based on established knowledge

claim: The reanalysis found 26 unique DEGs when considering the six cell types used by Mathys et al. using pseudobulk DE approach on the authors' original processed data.
source: Here, to compare the effect of the different DE approaches in isolation, we apply a pseudobulk DE approach (Chen et al., 2016) to the authors' original processed data. We found 26 unique DEGs when considering the six cell types used by the authors (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis data presented in Table 2

claim: The 26 DEGs found in the reanalysis was 549 times fewer DEGs than that reported originally at an FDR of 0.05.
source: This was 549 times fewer DEGs than that reported originally at an FDR of 0.05.
evidence: Supported by comparison of reanalysis results to original study

claim: The absolute log2 fold change (LFC) of the reanalysis DEGs is 15 times larger than Mathys et al.'s DEGs; median LFC of 2.34 and 0.16.
source: When we compare these DEGs, we can see that the absolute log2 fold change (LFC) of our DEGs is 15 times larger than the authors'; median LFC of 2.34 and 0.16
evidence: Supported by comparison data from the reanalysis

claim: Mathys et al.'s DEGs have an FDR score 8000 times smaller than the reanalysis DEGs; median FDR of 2.89 × 10–7 and 0.002.
source: despite the authors' DEGs having an FDR score 8000 times smaller; median FDR of 2.89 × 10–7and 0.002 (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by comparison data shown in Figure 1

claim: There is a high correlation in the genes' fold change values across the pseudobulk analysis and Mathys et al.'s pseudoreplication analysis (Pearson R of 0.87 for an adjusted p-value of 0.05).
source: Although we examined a high correlation in the genes' fold change values across our pseudobulk analysis and the authors' pseudoreplication analysis (Pearson R of 0.87 for an adjusted p-value of 0.05, Table 3), the p-values and resulting DEGs vary considerably.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data presented in Table 3

claim: There is a near perfect, positive correlation between DEG and cell counts for Mathys et al.'s pseudoreplication analysis.
source: There is a near perfect, positive correlation between DEG and cell counts for the authors' pseudoreplication analysis (Figure 1c)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1c

claim: There is a near perfect, positive correlation between DEG and cell counts for the 1031 genes from Mathys et al.'s combinatorial approach.
source: and for the 1031 genes from the authors' combinatorial approach (Figure 1d)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1d

claim: The positive correlation between DEG and cell counts is not present in the pseudobulk reanalysis.
source: which is not present in our pseudobulk reanalysis (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1e

claim: Microglia is the primary cell type by which the genetic risk for AD acts.
source: In our opinion, it makes more sense to identify the majority of large effect size DEGs in microglia which recent work has established is the primary cell type by which the genetic risk for AD acts (Skene and Grant, 2016; McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Skene and Grant, 2016 and McQuade and Blurton-Jones, 2019

claim: 96% of all DEGs from the reanalysis were in microglia.
source: This is what we found with our pseudobulk DE approach – 96% of all DEGs were in microglia (Table 2)
evidence: Supported by reanalysis data presented in Table 2

claim: Only 3% of Mathys et al.'s DEGs were in microglia.
source: whereas only 3% of the authors' DEGs were in microglia.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the original study's results

claim: Pseudoreplication approaches result in false positives by artificially inflating the confidence from non-independent samples.
source: Although it has been proven that pseudoreplication approaches result in false positives by artificially inflating the confidence from non-independent samples
evidence: Based on established methodological knowledge

claim: The cell-level analysis approach with randomly permuted patient identifiers consistently found high numbers of DEGs.
source: We ran the same cell-level analysis approach – a Wilcoxon rank-sum test and FDR multiple-testing correction – 100 times whilst randomly permuting the patient identifiers (Figure 1f). We would expect to find minimal DEGs with this approach given the random mixing of case and control patients. However, this pseudoreplication approach consistently found high numbers of DEGs
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis data shown in Figure 1f

claim: The same correlation between the number of cells and the number of DEGs was observed with randomly permuted patient identifiers as with Mathys et al.'s results.
source: and we observe the same correlation between the number of cells and the number of DEGs as with the authors' results.
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis data

claim: The correlation between cell counts and DEGs was not observed when running the same permutation analysis with pseudobulk DE.
source: We did not observe the same pattern when running the same analysis with pseudobulk DE (Figure 1g).
evidence: Supported by permutation analysis data shown in Figure 1g

claim: Integrating pseudoreplication approach with a mixed model artificially inflates the test confidence for a random sample of the genes resulting in more false discoveries in cell types with bigger counts.
source: As a result, we conclude that integrating this pseudoreplication approach with a mixed model like the authors proposed just artificially inflates the test confidence for a random sample of the genes resulting in more false discoveries in cell types with bigger counts.
evidence: Based on inference from the permutation analysis results

claim: Pseudobulk DE on the reprocessed data found 16 unique DEGs.
source: We also performed pseudobulk DE on our reprocessed data and found 16 unique DEGs (Table 4).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis data presented in Table 4

claim: The fold change correlation between the two DE analyses (reprocessed data vs authors' processed data) on the identified DEGs is only moderate (Pearson R of 0.57).
source: It is worth noting that the fold change correlation between our two DE analyses (reprocessed data vs authors' processed data) on the identified DEGs is only moderate (Pearson R of 0.57)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis between the two reanalysis approaches

claim: The fold change correlation between reprocessed and original processed data (0.57) is lower than that of the correlation between pseudoreplication and pseudobulk on the same dataset.
source: and is lower than that of the correlation between pseudoreplication and pseudobulk on the same dataset (Table 3).

claim: Low quality high mitochondrial read cells have an effect on DE analysis.
source: This highlights the effect that the low quality high mitochondrial read cells have on DE analysis.

claim: The use of pseudoreplication in neuroscience research is not isolated to Mathys et al.'s work; others have used this approach.
source: However, we would like to highlight that the use of pseudoreplication in neuroscience research is not isolated to the authors' work; others have used this approach (Fernandes et al., 2020; Lui et al., 2021; Wakhloo et al., 2020), and their results should be similarly scrutinised.
